raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old man was attended in the dental clinic complaining of symptomatic oral lesions with two months in duration. The intraoral physical examination revealed diffuse, friable, vegetative areas on the right upper alveolar ridge, hard palate, and left inferior alveolar ridge (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)). His medical history revealed a diagnosis of tuberculosis about a month ago in which the expectorated sputum smears were positive for bacteria and acid-fast bacilli. In addition, at the time of diagnosis of tuberculosis, the patient had a significant weight loss and asthenia. The patient was under antibacterial therapy (oral isoniazid (INH) 225 mg/day, rifampicin (RFP) 450 mg/day, pyrazinamide 1,200 mg/day, and ethambutol (EB) 825 mg/day). Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection was negative. Furthermore, the patient confirmed smoking and chronic alcoholism. He worked as a night flow controller on the side of a highway and lived very close to the countryside. After knowing the patient's medical history, the main hypothesis for oral lesions was tuberculosis.
An incisional biopsy of the right upper alveolar ridge showed connective tissue with intense inflammatory infiltrate with a granulomatous pattern, consisting of giant multinucleated inflammatory cells and vacuolated macrophages, with innumerable fungi suggestive of H. capsulatum (Figures 2(a) and 2(b)). Staining slides with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) (Figures 2(c) and 2(d)) and Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver were positive for the morphological characteristics of H. capsulatum. In addition, the immunohistochemical reactivity to Histoplasma using polyclonal antibody was positive; for polyclonal P. brasiliensis, Leishmania spp. and Calmette-Guerin bacillus were negative. The diagnosis of oral histoplasmosis was established. We did not search for fungi in other biological samples.
Initially, the drug was maintained for tuberculosis and prescribed fluconazol (400 mg/day) for seven months for treatment of oral histoplasmosis. During the follow-up, when a gradual increase in body weight was noted, fluconazole was substituted for itraconazole 200 mg/day for eight months with the resolution of oral histoplasmosis lesions. The clinical control one year after initiation of itraconazole treatment can be seen in Figures 3(a) and 3(b). One year after the initial treatment of tuberculosis, the patient was cured.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male presented with painful, vegetative oral lesions persisting for two months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-month history of symptomatic, progressively expanding oral mucosal lesions. He had been diagnosed with a pulmonary infection 1 month prior accompanied by significant weight loss and asthenia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with a pulmonary mycobacterial/respiratory infection 1 month prior, on a four-drug antimicrobial regimen (isoniazid 225 mg/day, rifampicin 450 mg/day, pyrazinamide 1,200 mg/day, and ethambutol 825 mg/day). History of cigarette smoking and chronic alcoholism. Works as a night traffic controller near the countryside.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported oral pain, weight loss, and asthenia. Home medications: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Intraoral examination revealed diffuse, friable, vegetative mucosal lesions over the right upper alveolar ridge, hard palate, and left inferior alveolar ridge.
objective.advanced_workup: Incisional biopsy of the right upper alveolar ridge: demonstrated connective tissue with an intense granulomatous inflammatory infiltrate, multinucleated giant cells, and vacuolated macrophages with intracellular budding yeasts; periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver stains were positive for fungal organisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Oral histoplasmosis (Histoplasma capsulatum) occurring concurrently with active pulmonary tuberculosis. Sputum smears 1 month prior were positive for acid-fast bacilli confirming pulmonary tuberculosis. Oral lesion biopsy demonstrated intense granulomatous inflammation with yeasts morphologically consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum; immunohistochemistry was positive for polyclonal Histoplasma antibody, and negative for Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, Leishmania spp., and BCG.
Treatment & Outcome: Maintained antitubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol). Treated for oral histoplasmosis with oral fluconazole (400 mg/day) for 7 months, followed by itraconazole (200 mg/day) for 8 months. Complete healing of oral mucosal lesions was achieved, and the patient was confirmed cured of tuberculosis and histoplasmosis at one-year follow-up.
